questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

The children is crying loudly because they have lost all their favorite toys.
questions.explanation: The error lies in 'is crying loudly'. 'Children' is a plural noun, so it must take a plural verb. The correct phrase should be 'The children are crying loudly' to maintain proper subject-verb agreement.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Neither of the two boys have brought their respective mathematics textbooks to the class.
questions.explanation: The error is in the segment 'have brought their'. The pronoun 'Neither' acts as a singular subject and must be followed by a singular verb and singular possessive pronoun. It should be corrected to 'has brought his'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Hardly had I reached the railway station than the express train departed from the platform.
questions.explanation: The error lies in the use of 'than'. The adverb 'hardly' is always paired with the conjunction 'when', not 'than'. ('No sooner' is paired with 'than'). The correct sentence is 'Hardly had I reached the railway station when the express train departed...'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Unless you do not work hard, you will definitely fail the upcoming board examination.
questions.explanation: The error is 'do not work hard'. The word 'unless' inherently carries a negative meaning ('if not'). Using 'not' along with 'unless' in the same clause creates a double negative. It should correctly be 'Unless you work hard...'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

One of my best friend is going to travel to the United States next month.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'One of' must always be followed by a plural noun, because you are selecting one from a group of many. The singular verb 'is' correctly matches 'One', but 'friend' must be pluralized. It should be 'One of my best friends'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

The inquiry committee were divided in its opinion regarding the final verdict of the case.
questions.explanation: When a collective noun like 'committee' is divided in opinion, it is treated as plural (hence 'were divided' is correct). However, the pronoun must also match the plural nature. 'its opinion' should be corrected to 'their opinions'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Despite lacking formal education, he is clearly more smarter than his younger brother.
questions.explanation: The error lies in the phrase 'more smarter'. The word 'smarter' is already the comparative degree of 'smart'. Adding 'more' creates an incorrect double comparative. It should simply be 'smarter than'.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

He has been living in this city (A) since the last twenty years (B) and has not thought about (C) shifting to another place (D).

options.option_text: He has been living in this city

questions.explanation: With present perfect continuous tense expressing duration, 'for' is used (e.g., 'for twenty years'), not 'since'. 'Since' marks a specific point in time (e.g., 'since 2005'), not a span. Replace 'since' with 'for'. Segment D is a grammatically valid gerund complement and is not the error.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

The new mountain expressway (A) is more wider than the old road (B) and has cut down travel time (C) to the district headquarters (D).

options.option_text: is more wider than the old road
and has cut down travel time

questions.explanation: 'More wider' is a double comparative — it incorrectly combines the '-er' suffix with 'more' for the same adjective. The correct form is simply 'wider'. SSC/bank exams regularly test this error. Option A ('The new mountain expressway') is a valid noun phrase and contains no error.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

If the government would have (A) invested more in rural roads (B) the poverty levels in these areas (C) would have declined noticeably (D).

options.option_text: the poverty levels in these areas

questions.explanation: In a third conditional (unreal past), the if-clause must use the past perfect ('had invested'), never 'would have'. Using 'would have' in the if-clause is a very common error in Indian English. Segment D ('would have declined') is the correct result-clause construction and is not the error.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

The officer was accustomed with (A) working in difficult conditions (B) and never sought any leave (C) during the entire posting period (D).
questions.explanation: 'Accustomed' must be followed by 'to', not 'with'. The correct phrase is 'accustomed to working'. This preposition error is a high-frequency trap in SSC/IBPS papers. Segment C ('never sought any leave') may attract attention, but 'sought' is the correct past tense of 'seek' and the clause is sound.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

After the exhausting journey from Delhi (A) he laid on the floor of the rest house (B) for several hours before he could (C) resume his duties the next morning (D).

options.option_text: After the exhausting journey from Delhi
he laid on the floor of the rest house
for several hours before he could
resume his duties the next morning

questions.explanation: 'Laid' is the past tense of the transitive verb 'lay' (to place something). When meaning 'to recline', the intransitive verb 'lie' is needed — its past tense is 'lay'. So the correct form is 'he lay on the floor'. The lay/lie/laid confusion is a classic SSC and IBPS PO trap. Segment A is a correct adverbial phrase.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

The tribunal recommended that (A) the defaulting firm pays a fine (B) of fifty lakh rupees in total (C) to the affected workers forthwith (D).

options.option_text: the defaulting firm pays a fine
of fifty lakh rupees in total

questions.explanation: After verbs of recommendation, suggestion, demand, or insistence (recommend, suggest, demand, insist), the verb in the 'that-clause' must be the bare infinitive (subjunctive mood) regardless of subject. So 'pays' must be 'pay': '...that the defaulting firm pay a fine'. This subjunctive rule is a high-frequency and frequently missed error in banking exams. Segment A is structurally correct.

questions.stem:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

No sooner had the Finance Minister (A) announced the new budget proposals (B) when the protests suddenly erupted (C) across several major cities of India (D).

options.option_text: No sooner had the Finance Minister
across several major cities of India

questions.explanation: The correlative conjunction 'no sooner' must always pair with 'than', never 'when'. Correct: 'No sooner had...than...'. This is distinct from 'hardly/scarcely', which pair with 'when' or 'before'. Candidates who confuse the two families of negative adverbs routinely pick the wrong segment. Segment A is correct — 'no sooner' triggers subject-auxiliary inversion ('had the Finance Minister').
